‘When China wants to do something, boy, they move fast.’
The electrolyzer has come a long way in the nearly 250 years since a pair of Dutch scientists first used electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. Over the decades, European and American scientists refined and commercialized this technology, yet it is China that now accounts for nearly 70% of global electrolyzer manufacturing capacity, churning out the machines that make clean hydrogen from water at a fraction of Western costs. Its factories are building far more equipment than its domestic hydrogen market can absorb, and exports are climbing. On paper, China looks poised to dominate the global electrolyzer and green hydrogen markets, much as it already has solar panels and batteries.
“It stands to reason that the Chinese would want to capture the market just like they did everything else,” Rinaldo Brutoco, a hydrogen investor and founder of the think tank World Business Academy, told me. Beijing’s latest Five-Year Plan certainly lends credence to that ambition, repeatedly calling for the development of green hydrogen, hydrogen-derived fuels, and electrolyzers, even as other nations lag behind their once-ambitious clean hydrogen targets.
But it’s not actually obvious that the technology will go the way of solar. For one, Western governments are increasingly wary of dependence on Chinese energy technologies and are trying to bolster domestic manufacturing and limit foreign competition through measures like tariffs, domestic-content bonuses, and subsidy eligibility restrictions . The West also specializes in its own electrolyzer tech, which relies on proton exchange membranes. Though more expensive than China’s typical alkaline electrolyzers, PEM systems pair better with intermittent renewable power.
China’s tech is improving , though, and its electrolyzer stacks — the pile of cells where water splits into hydrogen and oxygen — cost about 60% less than Western alternatives. But the stack only accounts for about 6% to 9% of the total levelised cost of clean hydrogen production; most of the expense comes from electrical and process equipment, labor, and, most importantly, clean electricity. That single-digit cost advantage may not be enough to sway foreign buyers, especially since some cheaper designs come with trade-offs in efficiency, lifecycle, and warranty coverage.
“When the project as a whole is considered, there’s a lot less deviation between the Chinese technology and the rest of the world’s,” Thomas Koller, regional hydrogen lead at the Norwegian energy and maritime consultancy DNV, told me. But China is working on that, he added. “They’re very competitive already on the stack. But now they know that they also want to be competitive on how that stack can integrate with the wider electrolyzer system.”
Cracking that system-level cost issue could bring China much closer to achieving global market dominance. DNV calculates that to meet the Paris Agreement’s targets, clean hydrogen would need to supply around 15% of global energy demand by 2050 — and the production equipment and resultant clean molecules would have to come from somewhere .
In the meantime, however, the analysts I spoke with agreed that China’s domestic green hydrogen market is positioned for a near-term boom, as the government pushes adoption across fertilizer, chemicals, oil refining, steel, and transportation. “Demand is really the key takeaway that I see from this new Five-Year Plan — shifting from production to thinking about demand,” Koller told me.
And while the plan was pretty much complete before the Iran war broke out, the ongoing disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has underscored the logic behind China’s hydrogen push, as the country previously relied on the Strait for up to half of its crude oil imports. “It’s placed them in a pretty good position — in respect of hydrogen at least — to try and strengthen one of these areas that can reduce dependence on imported oil,” Koller said of the Five-Year Plan.
China is already the world’s largest hydrogen producer and consumer by a wide margin, using the gas as a key industrial feedstock for its vast chemicals and heavy industry sectors. But today, the industry makes nearly all of that hydrogen with fossil fuels.
Beijing made clear in its latest Five-Year Plan, released in March, that it wants to change that. According to an unofficial translation, the state promised to “expand applications of hydrogen energy in transportation, electricity, industrial, and other domains,” while improving “renewable energy hydrogen production equipment” and advancing “the hydrogen energy industry chain toward green ammonia, methanol, and sustainable aviation fuels.” (China has not published an official English translation of the plan.)
The country certainly has the manufacturing capacity to support these ambitions. After hundreds of manufacturers poured into the electrolyzer industry earlier this decade, China now produces about 35 gigawatts worth of this equipment annually, compared with less than 2 gigawatts of domestic demand. The resulting glut has even led some producers to sell their equipment below cost, echoing the dynamics of the solar industry in the early 2010s. Now, Beijing is trying to build a green hydrogen market to soak up the surplus, elevating production of the fuel — and derivatives like ammonia, methanol, and SAF — to a national priority.
“They’re talking about nationwide pipelines for hydrogen. They’re talking about a regionalized cluster strategy; they have very hard targets for green hydrogen sales,” Brutoco told me.
China is targeting 2 million metric tons of renewable hydrogen production annually by 2030, an eightfold increase from roughly 0.25 million metric tons today. The government has also designated five city clusters as green hydrogen demonstration zones, each eligible for up to about $240 million over four years to scale up the fuel’s use across sectors including transportation, metallurgy, and green ammonia and methanol production — and to build the pipelines required to move it.
“Hydrogen has clearly moved up in political visibility,” Qi Qin, a China analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, told me back in March.
All of this stands in stark contrast to Western markets, where low-carbon hydrogen projects continue to be delayed or scrapped amid weak demand and waning political support. Clean hydrogen is still far more expensive than its fossil fuel-based counterpa

articles.title_orig: Spain train crash kills at least 68 as witnesses describe devastating scenes
articles.title_zh: Spain train crash kills at least 68 as witnesses describe devastating scenes
articles.content_orig:
A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped in central Spain , derailing two cars and killing at least 68 people Wednesday morning, according to local authorities.
The regional government of Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people were receiving medical treatment at hospitals. Rescue workers continue searching the wreckage for survivors and bodies.
The crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo, according to Spain's rail system operator ADIF. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.
Padilla told state broadcaster TVE the accident was between two high-speed trains heading in the same direction from Madrid to Seville and that one ran into the tail of the other while it was stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track.
The accident involved a train from Spain's state-owned RENFE company and the private rail company IRYO. Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January. Padilla said 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers were in the IRYO train.
"Today all of Spain is grieving," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said from the crash site, where he announced that his government would declare three days of national mourning.
Sánchez called for increased safety measures to restore confidence in a high-speed rail system that was once a source of national pride.
"It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year," said Sánchez, who faces a national election on Nov. 29.
Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said the crash was caused by what he called the "inexplicable" order from a central command center for Spain's trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.
Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. But the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stopped IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.
Puente said the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a "stop signal" active on that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.
Authorities were still studying information to see how fast the train was going, but it could have been at 200 kph (124 mph) for that stretch of the track, Puente said.
"I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts," Puente said.
The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left carriages shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.
Spanish Health Minister Mónica García said that emergency workers were focused on rescuing survivors and bodies from the most damaged train cars.
"It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy," García said.
Passenger Ignacio Relaño was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO.
"We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact," he said. "The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook."
Another passenger recounted to Cadena Ser radio how she felt the train slam on the brakes and was thrown forward in her seat, breaking the small table in front of her. She said she saw body parts and trapped people covered in blood.
The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, told Spanish state broadcaster TVE that civil protection authorities had asked his town hall to prepare a sports pavilion to attend to passengers.
In January, 45 people died in southern Spain when a train jumped the track and hit an oncoming train. The crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people. The January incident shook the confidence the European country has in its extensive high-speed rail network.

articles.title_orig: Fed Meeting Live Updates: Interest Rates Hold Steady Despite 'Elevated' Inflation
articles.title_zh: Fed Meeting Live Updates: Interest Rates Hold Steady Despite 'Elevated' Inflation
articles.content_orig:
The move comes just days ahead of the US midterm elections, in which the rising cost of living has been a key issue
The US Federal Reserve on Wednesday held interest rates steady, in line with market expectations, days ahead of crucial midterm elections where surging inflation has been a key issue.
The 12-member Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 to hold rates at a target range between 3.75 to 4.00 per cent, citing the need for more data in the fight against inflation, after having hiked for the first time in three years at its previous meeting in September.
“The accumulation of more information will help the committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the committee’s 2 per cent goal,” the Fed said in a statement announcing its decision.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft Reports Quarterly Cloud Sales That Beat Estimates
articles.title_zh: Microsoft Reports Quarterly Cloud Sales That Beat Estimates
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft shares rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business.
Here's how the company fared relative to LSEG consensus:
Microsoft's revenue grew 19% year over year in the quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, according to a statement , with Azure now its biggest single business.
The software giant has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to meet artificial intelligence demand, while also maintaining positive free cash flow unlike its fellow hyperscalers. Microsoft reported  $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30% from a year earlier. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion.
Microsoft flagged a higher growth rate for cash paid for property and equipment than overall capital expenditures, which include finance leases, because of "timing differences between receipt of goods and payment and a lower mix of finance leases."
Around 75% of capital expenditures are now tied to short-lived assets such as Intel chips and Nvidia graphics processing units, up from about 66% in the past three quarters and half in the year-ago quarter. The shift indicates Microsoft's prioritization of infrastructure it can can quickly turn into revenue.
Free cash flow declined 27% to $18.63 billion. Cloud rival Alphabet reported more than $9 billion in negative free cash flow in the quarter after Meta said last week its cash flow turned negative for the first time.
Microsoft's net income increased to $36.63 billion, or $4.92 per share, from $27.75 billion, or $3.72 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude a roughly $200 million loss on its investment in OpenAI.
For the first time, Microsoft disclosed revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars, at $33.17 billion in the quarter. Analysts polled by StreetAccount expected $32.32 billion. The growth rate in the June quarter was 42%.
Microsoft reported results under two operating segments — Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.  For the past 11 years, the company had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses.
In Agents and Infra, revenue rose almost 25% to $76.8 billion, more than the $75.63 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. The segment contains Azure, along with Microsoft 365 cloud products, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions and frontier and support services.
Revenue in the Devices and Consumer business slipped 3% to $15.48 billion, beating the StreetAccount consensus of $15.05 billion. The unit includes search and advertising, Xbox, devices and Windows operating system licenses sold to device makers.
Sales of devices and Windows licenses declined 22%, as higher memory and storage costs elevated prices.
As of Wednesday's close, Microsoft shares were up about 10% year to date, trailing the S&P 500 index, which has gained 13% over the same period.
During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft said it would cut 4,800 jobs , and followed up by announcing on Monday that it's offering buyouts to up to 60,000 employees, as it strives to balance a costly AI build-out with capital efficiency. Microsoft also established, during the quarter, an AI implementation unit and revealed a Copilot AI "super app" with coding abilities.
This story is developing. Please check back for updates.

Fed chair Kevin Warsh said politics played no role in pause of interest rate hikes, despite inflation remaining above 3%
The US Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged on Wednesday during its last board meeting before the midterm elections, keeping rates at one of the highest pre-election levels seen in over 20 years.
Two out of 12 board members voted against the pause, preferring to raise rates by a quarter point this meeting, the Fed board said in a statement.
Last month, Fed officials raised rates for the first time since 2023, citing rising inflation, bringing rates to a range of 3.75% to 4%. Inflation has hovered for years above the Fed’s target rate of 2%, and for most of this year, the annualized inflation rate has remained above 3%.
Though inflation rose higher in September, going from 3.4% in August to 3.7%, the pause signals the central bank is taking a wait-and-see approach ahead of the midterms next week.
During a press conference on Wednesday afternoon, the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, told reporters that the upcoming election played no role in deliberations.
“Politics played no role in the decision,” he said. “I didn’t hear an utterance about politics.”
The central bank is still focused on price stability, he said, but emphasized that “the information that we receive over the coming period will help us determine where want policy to be”.
“The period right in front of us is information rich, there’s a lot that’s happening in the world, my colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it,” he said.
September’s rate hike infuriated Donald Trump, who said that “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less”.
Warsh declined to comment on a remark from Donald Trump that, besides Warsh, the Fed board is full of Democratic-appointed members who “would like to see the country do badly”, but said that the latest meeting was “a heck of a family fight”.
“I’m honored to be here, and I’m honored to be chairman of this group,” he said.
Interest rates determine the cost of interest for loans, including for credit cards, mortgage and some savings accounts. During times of high inflation, raising rates can slow price increases.
Multiple Fed leaders have suggested in recent weeks that the central bank has room for a pause, even if most Fed economists are predicting one more rate hike before the end of the year.
“The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time,” the Fed governor Christopher Waller said earlier this month.
The proximity of the election also made it more likely that the Fed will “not take any radical action”, said Nicholas Economides, a professor of economics at the NYU Stern Business School.
“Even if the Fed were to do something radically different, the economy would not have time to adjust before the elections,” he said.
Rising prices this year have largely been driven by war in the Middle East with Iran. Oil prices have soared with the closure of the strait of Hormuz, a crucial passageway for trade. Inflation rose last month to its highest level since the spring, while oil traded briefly above $117 a barrel earlier this week, its highest price in more than six months.
The higher cost of living is expected to play a crucial role in the upcoming midterm elections that will determine which party will control Congress. Across multiple polls, the economy has been cited as the top issue for voters.
By itself, hiking interest rates cannot solely address inflation caused by supply shocks, Economides said. Raising rates is helpful for when the economy is too hot, or when demand outpaces supply, but can be counterproductive otherwise.
“If inflation is caused by supply factors, it doesn’t make sense to try to cure it by increasing interest rates because it won’t work,” he said. “It will slow down the economy at a time in which you don’t want it to slow down.
On Wednesday, Warsh also announced upcoming changes to the Fed’s eight board meetings it conducts annually. Starting in fall 2027, only seven of those meetings will be convened to set interest rates. That number will go down to six in 2028, with the other meetings dedicated to “broad monetary policy” when the change is implemented.

articles.title_orig: A US-China-Russia Summit: What’s at Stake? - Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA)
articles.title_zh: A US-China-Russia Summit: What’s at Stake? - Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA)
articles.content_orig:
Carney backs EU-Canada associate membership amid Trump tariff threats
Canada is set to host a summit with the European Union to bolster bilateral strategic and economic ties as its relations with its southern neighbour, the United States, are in sharp decline.
The summit is scheduled for October 29 to 30 in Canada’s French-speaking city of Montreal, and is expected to focus on closer cooperation on trade, technology, defence, energy, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, research and financial services.
In September, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed opening the door for Canada to become the EU’s first “associate member”; Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the move.
This will be the 21st Canada-EU summit and is expected to build on the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), which entered into force in 2017. It eliminates duties on up to 99 percent of all imported goods between the two sides, according to the European Council.
“In Montreal, we will take our partnership to the next level by launching our ‘Alliance for the Future’ to deepen our political, economic and institutional ties even further,” said European Council President Antonio Costa, who will be attending the summit along with Carney and von der Leyen. They are expected to issue a joint statement.
The deepening Canada-EU alignment seems fuelled by US President Donald Trump’s policies , which imposed hefty tariffs on both Canadian and European exports to the US and pushed Canada to look for ways to reduce its economic dependence on the US. Before Trump’s tariffs whipsawed relations, Canada sent nearly 80 percent of its exports to the US.
In August, trade talks between Ottawa and Washington, DC, broke down, and Trump imposed a 50 percent levy on $20bn of Canadian goods, or 5.5 percent of its exports. Canada responded with equivalent tariffs on US steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.
Both sides are seeking opportunities that will open more options beyond the world’s largest economy.
“The opportunity is clear. The EU brings market power, research depth, and manufacturing strength. Canada brings abundant energy, critical minerals, world-class capabilities in space, artificial intelligence (AI), and quantum, and one of the world’s strongest banking systems,” Carney’s office said in a statement.
The summit will give the two sides a chance to turn these “complementary strengths into concrete benefits for our peoples,” the statement added.
Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a think tank in Ottawa, Canada, sees benefits and challenges.
“These fields could be beneficial for both sides, and we are likely to see specific announcements during the summit on these sectors,” she told Al Jazeera.
“The main challenge is how quickly the political momentum can turn into specific deals and projects to deliver specific economic results,” she added.
The EU describes Canada as “the only non-European country” taking part in Security Action for Europe (SAFE), the EU’s 150 billion-euro ($167bn) loan programme that supports and expedites defence procurement by EU member states.
The EU concluded its agreement with Canada, allowing it to participate under SAFE, in February, and it gives Canadian firms preferential access and treatment in defence procurements financed by the SAFE Instrument.
Last month, von der Leyen proposed that Canada could become the EU’s first associate member, suggesting a deeper relationship spanning trade, technology, defence and economic security.
Carney later welcomed the proposal’s ambition, describing his goal as a “unique alliance” rather than conventional EU membership.
However, the term “ associate member ” does not currently exist in EU treaties or its standard enlargement framework, according to the Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS), a Brussels-based think tank.
“The term does not actually matter; what is important is the practical deepening of the relationship and the actual results, no matter what the final term is,” Nadjibulla said.
“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” von der Leyen said in her address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg last month, which Carney attended, making him the first foreign head of government to attend the annual “State of the European Union” address.
“I do not see that as an anti-US coalition. It is rather about diversification of economic and defence partnerships and building resilience for Canada. It is a continuation of Canadian Prime Minister Carney’s policies to create opportunities. A deeper alliance with Europe is essential to this agenda,” she said.
“President Trump will likely not appreciate this, but it is about Canada having more choices in an unpredictable world,” she added.
Bob Rae, former premier of Ontario and Canada’s ambassador to the United Nations from 2020 to 2025, told Al Jazeera that “President Trump does not control our policy. We have been having long and productive relations with the Europeans for hundreds of years, but Trump chose to treat Canada in a way that does not respect our sovereignty”.
He added that “engaging in conversations with the EU is perfectly normal and is not directed at the US”.
Trump has threatened the European Union with new tariffs over its proposal to make Canada the bloc’s first “associate member”, suggesting the move could be considered hostile to the US.
“If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe,” Trump told reporters in Charlotte, North Carolina, in September.
Trump dismissed the prospect of Canada joining the EU as “laughable” and called the US’s northern neighbour a “terrible trade partner”.

articles.title_orig: At least 68 people dead in Spain's second major train crash this year
articles.title_zh: At least 68 people dead in Spain's second major train crash this year
articles.content_orig:
At least 68 people have been killed in a collision between two trains in the Spanish province of Toledo, authorities have said.
The high-speed trains collided shortly before 9:15 a.m. local time (4:15 a.m. ET), when emergency services were deployed to the scene. It occurred on the Madrid to Seville line.
Transport Minister Óscar Puente told reporters in Madrid that the control system at the nearby town of Urda failed and six trains were stopped. One was allowed to restart and travelled 25km before hitting a stopped train at high speed, he added, saying it was "inexplicable" how this had happened.
As well as those killed, 50 people were also injured, the minister said.
Railway infrastructure manager Adif is investigating the sequence of events surrounding the accident, Spanish news agency EFE reported .
The local Castilla-La Mancha government confirmed at least 68 people had died, higher than another high-speed crash in southern Spain that killed 45 people in January.
Emiliano García-Page, the president of the region, said 24 people had died on a train operated by rail company Renfe, with the rest killed on a train operated by Iryo.
More than 500 passengers were on board the two trains, newspaper El País said.
Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by the Renfe train, saying the cause was "still unknown".
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said in a post on X that he was "shocked" by the accident.
"If there has been any negligence, it will come to light," he later said at a press conference.
"If there have been failures in the safety system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness. It is clear that we have experienced two terrible tragedies involving high-speed rail within the same year."
Sanchez's political future will be tested in a snap election on Nov. 29, which he called following widespread unrest over Spain's housing crisis.
Santiago Abascal, leader of the far-right Vox party — which is expected to make gains when Spain goes to the polls — pointed the finger at Sanchez's government over the train accident on Wednesday.
"Tragedy again. Rage again over the neglect, the ruin, and the betrayal suffered by the Spanish people," he said in a post on X.
— CNBC's Charlotte Reed contributed to this article.

Vladimir Putin hailed Elon Musk as a “genius” and said he was in contact with the tech billionaire as Russia develops its answer to his ⁠ Starlink satellite internet system.
It comes just weeks after Ukraine , which uses a version of Starlink as a key component of drone operations and battlefield communications , complained of speed restrictions that hampered its ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forced the cancellation of some operations.
The Russian president made the remark about Mr Musk on Wednesday as he listened to a presentation by digital development minister Maksut Shadayev, ⁠who said Russia had launched more than 30 satellites ​as ⁠it builds its own Starlink equivalent.
"Just a second, I want to point out this is just our first step. Elon Musk is a genius, he's just a real genius," said Mr Putin.
Mr Shadayev ‌said in reply to a question from Mr Putin that Mr Musk had more than 5,000 low-orbit satellites up and running — although the actual number is close to 10,000, according to independent tracking site ‌Orbital Radar.
"Over 5,000 while we are only taking our first steps. But we are proud that we have begun to do this, and started to do it independently," Mr Putin said, adding that the task now was "to move from quality to quantity".
"We are in close contact with our American partners — including ⁠Mr Musk — because it is very important, in orbit, not to get in each other's way and to maintain a certain level of discipline and order," he said.
Starlink, which does not work in Russia, uses a constellation of satellites that orbit far lower than traditional geostationary communications satellites, reducing signal travel time.
Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky earlier this month accused the United States of withdrawing vital intelligence and weakening the Starlink service at a crucial time in the Russian invasion.
Starshield - the military version of Starlink - has provided a lifeline to Ukraine in helping to defend against incoming attacks , as well as striking Russian targets.
However, on October 14, Ukrainian officials began reporting trouble with terminals moving at speed.
The problems with Starlink in Ukraine added to tensions between Kyiv and the US after Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel.
He also pressed the country to stop striking Russian oil refineries and saying it was time for Ukrainians to replace their president.
At the weekend, Ukraine said Starlink and Starshield were again ⁠fully functional, but Musk accused the Ukrainian military of violating SpaceX 's terms.
Neither Mr Musk nor the US government, which operates Starshield ‌using Starlink technology, have ​taken responsibility for imposing the speed curbs.
Russian officials have spoken highly of Mr Musk before. In 2025, Putin's investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev said Russia would like to work with him on a mission to Mars.

articles.title_zh: Wendy’s, struggling with beef prices and growing competition, gets a buyout offer
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Struggling burger chain Wendy’s has received a buyout offer from noted investor Nelson Peltz.
The buyout offer comes after Wendy’s shares dropped roughly 70% over the past five years, per the Wall Street Journal. Peltz argues that the fast food giant would be better off as a private company and offered to pay around $1.4 billion.
The chain, founded in 1969 by Dave Thomas and named after his daughter, is known for its square burgers and Frosty desserts. Same-store sales, or sales at restaurants open at least a year, have declined for more than two years. Those sales fell during the first two quarters of 2026.
Peltz’s Trian Fund Management and several partners are offering Wendy’s $7.35 per share in cash, or a premium of nearly 19% over the stock’s closing price on Tuesday.
Restaurant operator Flynn Group and investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners have partnered with Trian on the offer, according to WSJ .
In a letter to the company’s board of directors, Peltz said going private “will deliver the best outcome for the broader stakeholder base.”
“Wendy’s sits at a critical juncture," Peltz wrote. "The external environment has become increasingly challenging given the significant pressures on the U.S. consumer, economic uncertainty, persistent commodity inflation and intensifying competition, particularly within the QSR (quick service restaurant) burger category."
Peltz has invested in companies from Procter & Gamble and Disney, to DuPont. According to a regulatory document filed Wednesday, Trian’s stake in Wendy’s totals 16.3%.
Wendy’s, based in Dublin, Ohio, didn’t immediately comment. Restaurant industry heavyweight Robert Wright took over as the chain’s new president and CEO in May, replacing interim boss Kenneth Cook.
Wright previously ran sandwich chain Potbelly Corp and held top leadership roles at Wendy’s, Domino’s Pizza and Charleys Philly Steaks. He said in August that Wendy’s needs to improve its food, prices, customer experience and marketing to win customers back.
Wendy’s is scheduled to report its quarterly financial results next week. Analysts expect Wendy’s earned 9 cents per share on sales of $531 million on average.
Shares rose 91 cents to $7.05 Wednesday.

articles.title_orig: Stock market today: Nasdaq wavers, S&P 500 and Dow climb as Fed votes to hold rates steady in 10-2 decision
articles.title_zh: Stock market today: Nasdaq wavers, S&P 500 and Dow climb as Fed votes to hold rates steady in 10-2 decision
articles.content_orig:
Fed chair Kevin Warsh said politics played no role in pause of interest rate hikes, despite inflation remaining above 3%
The US Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged on Wednesday during its last board meeting before the midterm elections, keeping rates at one of the highest pre-election levels seen in over 20 years.
Two out of 12 board members voted against the pause, preferring to raise rates by a quarter point this meeting, the Fed board said in a statement.
Last month, Fed officials raised rates for the first time since 2023, citing rising inflation, bringing rates to a range of 3.75% to 4%. Inflation has hovered for years above the Fed’s target rate of 2%, and for most of this year, the annualized inflation rate has remained above 3%.
Though inflation rose higher in September, going from 3.4% in August to 3.7%, the pause signals the central bank is taking a wait-and-see approach ahead of the midterms next week.
During a press conference on Wednesday afternoon, the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, told reporters that the upcoming election played no role in deliberations.
“Politics played no role in the decision,” he said. “I didn’t hear an utterance about politics.”
The central bank is still focused on price stability, he said, but emphasized that “the information that we receive over the coming period will help us determine where want policy to be”.
“The period right in front of us is information rich, there’s a lot that’s happening in the world, my colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it,” he said.
September’s rate hike infuriated Donald Trump, who said that “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less”.
Warsh declined to comment on a remark from Donald Trump that, besides Warsh, the Fed board is full of Democratic-appointed members who “would like to see the country do badly”, but said that the latest meeting was “a heck of a family fight”.
“I’m honored to be here, and I’m honored to be chairman of this group,” he said.
Interest rates determine the cost of interest for loans, including for credit cards, mortgage and some savings accounts. During times of high inflation, raising rates can slow price increases.
Multiple Fed leaders have suggested in recent weeks that the central bank has room for a pause, even if most Fed economists are predicting one more rate hike before the end of the year.
“The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time,” the Fed governor Christopher Waller said earlier this month.
The proximity of the election also made it more likely that the Fed will “not take any radical action”, said Nicholas Economides, a professor of economics at the NYU Stern Business School.
“Even if the Fed were to do something radically different, the economy would not have time to adjust before the elections,” he said.
Rising prices this year have largely been driven by war in the Middle East with Iran. Oil prices have soared with the closure of the strait of Hormuz, a crucial passageway for trade. Inflation rose last month to its highest level since the spring, while oil traded briefly above $117 a barrel earlier this week, its highest price in more than six months.
The higher cost of living is expected to play a crucial role in the upcoming midterm elections that will determine which party will control Congress. Across multiple polls, the economy has been cited as the top issue for voters.
By itself, hiking interest rates cannot solely address inflation caused by supply shocks, Economides said. Raising rates is helpful for when the economy is too hot, or when demand outpaces supply, but can be counterproductive otherwise.
“If inflation is caused by supply factors, it doesn’t make sense to try to cure it by increasing interest rates because it won’t work,” he said. “It will slow down the economy at a time in which you don’t want it to slow down.
On Wednesday, Warsh also announced upcoming changes to the Fed’s eight board meetings it conducts annually. Starting in fall 2027, only seven of those meetings will be convened to set interest rates. That number will go down to six in 2028, with the other meetings dedicated to “broad monetary policy” when the change is implemented.

articles.title_orig: Residents on the doomed Villa Vie Odyssey cruise describe the first 24 hours after being kicked off in Cambodia
articles.title_zh: Residents on the doomed Villa Vie Odyssey cruise describe the first 24 hours after being kicked off in Cambodia
articles.content_orig:
Passengers on a live-aboard round-the-world cruise say they were abruptly asked to leave the ship and given only hours to disembark.
Villa Vie Residences, which operates the residential cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey , said on Tuesday it had halted operations due to surging fuel costs.
The ship was docked at the port of Sihanoukville in Cambodia when the announcement was made, with passengers saying they were given only eight hours to disembark.
"On October 27, 2026, we received notice from the CEO at around 6 a.m. that all residents had to disembark by 2 p.m. that day," passengers Lanette Canen and John Bodin told Business Insider by email.
Canen and Bodin have been on the Odyssey since it first set sail in September 2024 and run a YouTube channel called Living Life on a Cruise about their experiences on board.
"We knew leaving was a possibility, but the eight-hour notice still surprised us," they said.
The couple shared a video on their YouTube channel that appears to show the moment a staff member announced that passengers must leave the ship.
"Unfortunately, they were unable to secure the fuel necessary to continue operations," a male voice says in the video.
A notice on the Villa Vie Residences website says the company is working with residents to arrange temporary living arrangements and that it is evaluating restructuring options over the next 60 days.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Villa Vie Residences did not immediately respond to requests for comment. CEO Kathy Villalba and executive chairman Mikael Petterson did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Villa Vie Residences said in a statement on Tuesday that the surging cost of fuel since the beginning of the Iran war had made operating the cruise liner increasingly difficult.
The company said its monthly fuel expenses per cabin, which had previously averaged about $1,800, had risen as much as 344% in parts of Asia, to an estimated $6,000 to $8,000.
"Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port," Villa Vie Residences said.
"Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses."
On August 1, Villalba, the CEO, sent residents a message titled "Urgent operational update" on an internal messaging platform. In the message, she referenced a "fuel contribution" that had been previously requested of residents. Business Insider has viewed a screenshot of the message.
"When the fuel contribution was requested several months ago, participation was not universal," she wrote in the message. "The contributions received helped some, but they covered only part of the extraordinary increase in fuel costs."
Villalba wrote that the "cash-flow" challenge had continued, and the Odyssey needed 650 metric tons of fuel, adding that fuel prices had almost doubled.
"We have now reached a critical point. The lack of full participation, combined with the unprecedented increase in fuel costs, means we must make immediate and creative operational decisions to preserve the voyage," her message said.
It continued, "We are asking every Resident who did not previously contribute to please do so now. We are also asking those who are able to provide additional support to consider helping with this immediate fuel requirement."
Villalba described the financial need as "real, immediate, and necessary to keep Odyssey moving." It went on, "This is a moment when preserving our home and continuing the voyage requires support beyond contractual minimums from those who are able to provide it."
Among the passengers asked to disembark on Tuesday with only a few hours' notice was Barbara Fiegel, 62, who has lived with her partner aboard the ship since December 2024.
"Everybody's just shocked, everybody's just saddened by this whole issue," she said. "We're still processing, trying to debate what we're going to do."
Fiegel said she and her partner booked a hotel room in Cambodia, then returned to the ship Tuesday evening and Wednesday afternoon to empty their safe and pack their belongings. "Today, as we approached, as we went back on the shuttle back to the ship, I couldn't stop crying," she said.
They plan to return on Thursday to collect their remaining items. Fiegel described the atmosphere on the Odyssey as a “ghost town.”
Joel Greiff, 57, moved aboard the ship at the start of the month. “I was planning to live on the ship for 10, 20, or 73 years,” he said. “I don’t think that will be happening.”
When residents were told to disembark, Greiff emptied his cabin. “I personally grabbed everything,” he said.
He said he would like to return if Villa Vie Residences resumes operations. If not, he is planning to move to Thailand. In the meantime, he has rented an apartment in Cambodia for a month.
Greiff said he plans to return to the Odyssey on Thursday to assist other residents and “help with their luggage, help them find a place, and just start getting them and all their stuff off the ship.”
Have you spent any time on the Villa Vie Odyssey as a cabin owner, renter, or staff member? If you have a story to share, get in touch with this reporter: jzitser@businessinsider.com .

articles.title_orig: Kylian Mbappé’s China crisis shows how sensitive Mao’s legacy remains | Rebecca Bailey
articles.title_zh: Kylian Mbappé’s China crisis shows how sensitive Mao’s legacy remains | Rebecca Bailey
articles.content_orig:
Real Madrid forward was dropped by brands for comments Chinese media generally steered clear of outlining
I t’s been a bad start to the week for the Kylian Mbappé. The France forward missed out on joining the elite roster of Ballon d’Or winners and instead became the latest high-profile addition to a far less illustrious list – that of foreign brands and individuals charged with “hurting the feelings of the Chinese people”.
The saga began when a video of the Real Madrid player making light of a meme involving him and China’s former leader Mao Zedong began spreading.
Within hours Mbappé found himself condemned online, before being unceremoniously dropped by brands , then held responsible for state television suspending the entire top Spanish league from its schedule. On Tuesday Mbappé apologised – “My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China ” – as did La Liga, which released a statement saying it “deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé’s recent comments have caused among Chinese fans”.
Foreign brands from Mercedes to Versace and celebrities from John Cena to Katy Perry have previously been sent to the sin bin for crossing China’s political lines on Tibet, Hong Kong and Taiwan.
Mbappé’s case shows how sensitive Mao’s legacy remains in China 50 years after his death – to the extent that most Chinese coverage of the affair does not even mention what the footballer said.
In the video, Mbappé references a meme of himself and “a guy … I think he was a Chinese dictator”, before a composite image of Mbappé’s face on Mao’s body pops up. (Mbappé has been nicknamed “the dictator” since his time at Paris Saint-Germain, a joke referring to his perceived influence at the club.)
The football app Dongqiudi was among the first to release a statement condemning the “inappropriate remarks”, but said: “Because his comments were offensive to China and the Chinese people, we cannot translate them.” Chinese media have reported on reactions such as the brand desertions, and the China Football Association’s lodging of a “stern protest” with Real Madrid – who apologised on Wednesday “to the Chinese people for any offence caused” – but have generally steered clear of outlining Mbappé’s precise offence.
The topic was still trending on Chinese social media on Wednesday morning, with one hashtag relating to the superstar’s apology boasting more than 600m views. Some posts asked variations on a simple question: “What did he actually say?”
Manya Koetse, editor of the Eye on Digital China newsletter, said in a post on X: “Many netizens without a VPN are still left in the dark about why all the talk about boycotting Mbappé is actually happening.”
Still, many expressed anger at what was characterised as disrespect for, as well as a misunderstanding of, China’s history. “For the majority of the [Chinese] people, Mao was and is still not seen as negatively as it is believed in the west,” said Mobo Gao, professor of Chinese studies at Adelaide University.
Mao was the founding leader of modern China, but his legacy includes radical policies such as the Great Leap Forward, an industrialisation policy blamed for a famine that killed as many as 30 million people by some estimates.
The ruling Communist party (CCP) maintains Mao was a revolutionary hero, though after his death it acknowledged another extreme policy, the violent Cultural Revolution, was a “grave mistake”.
Gao said: “There has been intense tension between Mao hatred and Mao support among the Chinese themselves. This tension is even more keenly felt since the economy has slowed.”
after newsletter promotion
Some scholars have pointed to a resurgence of interest in Mao among younger Chinese, with a yearning for a time they regard as more idealistic and egalitarian – something the CCP is keen to keep in check.
Jennifer Pan, professor of communication at Stanford University, said the difficulty of doing independent social science surveys in the past decade meant “our understanding of what Chinese people actually think is weak”. Pan said: “Social media doesn’t fill that gap. It’s noisy, unrepresentative, and censored … What we see is that companies, platforms, broadcasters and the foreign ministry moved together quickly. Did this follow public anger, or did this produce public anger? Either is possible, and we can’t tell which came first.”
Whichever way round, the financial cost for Mbappé is the same. His face is a common sight on Chinese buses, in subways and in online ads, and his commercial deals could be worth “as much as $30m (£22.6m) per year”, said Mark Dreyer, author of Sporting Superpower, a book about China’s ambitions in the sector.
However, “as soon as someone else has decided you’ve crossed the line, it’s a race to who can cut ties quickest, who can be the most patriotic”, he said. “Then you have to kiss the ring – there really is no other way if you want to stay in the market.”
Mbappé’s and La Liga’s swift apologies suggest they are trying to avoid a fate like the NBA, whose lucrative pre-season matches were shut out of China for six years after the Houston Rockets’ then general manager Daryl Morey voiced support for Hong Kong pro-democracy protests in 2019.
La Liga may have better luck, with the state broadcaster CCTV saying it would listen to what Mbappé had to say, and “more importantly” watch what he does.
On Wednesday a foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, said: “We take seriously the apology the individual concerned has made.”
Dreyer said: “It doesn’t sound like it’s an instant ‘all is forgiven’. But it sounds like they’re going to be a little bit more, for want of a better word, reasonable.”

articles.title_orig: Fuel costs force US cruise ship to suspend multiyear voyage in Cambodia
articles.title_zh: Fuel costs force US cruise ship to suspend multiyear voyage in Cambodia
articles.content_orig:
A United States cruise ship has suspended its around-the-world voyage in Cambodia, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark with no confirmed departure date.
The MV Odyssey, operated by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, arrived at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on Friday. The company said monthly fuel expenses per cabin, which historically averaged $1,800, had climbed to an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia.
The company said it tried to reduce consumption by slowing the ship and spending more time in port but could not offset the rising costs.
“We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses,” Villa Vie Residences said in a statement on Tuesday, adding that passing the full increase on to residents was not a realistic solution.
Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has been curtailed since the United States-Israel war on Iran began, squeezing supplies of petroleum-based fuels and pushing up prices, particularly in Southeast Asia.
The ship was carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, and 156 crew members, Cambodian officials said. Some passengers said they received only seven hours notice to disembark and had to arrange their own accommodation.
Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from the US state of Wyoming who boarded the ship 17 months ago, said they had expected to live at sea for years. They said the company had already struggled with itinerary changes, unreliable internet and declining food quality.
“We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything,” Lynn Montoya said, alleging mismanagement and unpaid crew members.
Other passengers said they hoped a new company or a resident-led effort could save the venture.
Carol Larson, 69, who bought her cabin for $120,000 in instalments, said she did not regret taking the risk despite the suspension.
“I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising,” she said.
The ship set sail from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in October 2024 on a voyage originally planned to last three and a half years. Built in 1993, the ship was purchased by Villa Vie Residences in 2023 and offered cabins for long-term living with lifetime-vessel suites initially priced from about $230,000.
Cambodian officials said the ship was expected to refuel and leave on Saturday although the operator had not publicly confirmed a departure date.

Apple also released an updated version of its World Travel Adapter Kit that had disappeared from its online store in 2025, with U.S. pricing set at $39. Each of the international AC plugs included in the box now have the AC Connector 2 too.
Apple's power adapters have a removable plug, and the World Travel Adapter Kit contains various plug types for international travel:
The kit includes five interchangeable AC plugs: Type A: North America, Japan Type C: Continental Europe, Brazil Type D: India Type G: United Kingdom, United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Singapore Type I: Australia, New Zealand
In a new support document , Apple said its updated power adapters, extension cable, and plugs use the AC Connector 2 with a pill-shaped design to comply with "updated regulations." Apple's previous "AC Connector 1" has a notched design.
Apple began rolling out the AC Connector 2 in a few countries earlier this year, leading to some customers complaining about compatibility issues with Apple's older extension cables and World Travel Adapter Kit. Apple has now solved that problem by releasing these updated versions of the accessories with the AC Connector 2.

articles.title_orig: Lula’s Election Win in Brazil Is a Relief for China - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: Lula’s Election Win in Brazil Is a Relief for China - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva shakes hands with Chinese President Xi Jinping during a signing ceremony at the Great Hall of the People, Beijing, May 13, 2025.
On October 4, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva finished the first round of Brazil’s presidential election behind his main rival, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro and an open ally of U.S. President Donald Trump. Flavio Bolsonaro had taken 47 percent of valid votes against Lula’s 45 percent. Because no one topped 50 percent of votes, however, the race went to a second-round runoff.
The first post-election poll gave Bolsonaro a six-point lead in the head-to-head contest. Three weeks later, Lula won with 51.76 percent , a margin of roughly 4.3 million ballots, securing an unprecedented fourth term. His victory came after intense popular demonstrations in leading cities such as Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, and Belo Horizonte, as well as a new social media strategy boosted by political allies.
Lula’s comeback matters well beyond Brasília. Since late 2025, Latin America has seen a regional shift toward right-wing regimes. Bolivia, Chile, Honduras, Costa Rica, Colombia, and Peru all elected conservative governments, most of them endorsed by Washington.
Brazil was meant to be the crowning piece of Trump’s foreign policy, seeing as it is the largest market in the region and one of the only ones who did not agree on Trump’s Shield for the Americas initiative . Instead, Brazil has opted for a pragmatic foreign economic policy, trying to negotiate with both China and the United States.
The Donroe Doctrine Meets Its Limits
Washington’s strategy has been referred to as the “Donroe Doctrine,” claiming the United States’ right to assert its interests in the region in security terms. In practice that has meant rewarding ideological allies and treating Chinese influence as a central opposing force.
A series of electoral victories seemed to confirm the effectiveness of Trump’s approach to the region. Rodrigo Paz ended two decades of Movimiento al Socialismo (MAS) rule in Bolivia in October 2025. José Antonio Kast won Chile in December. Nasry Asfura took office in Honduras after Trump threatened to cut aid if he lost. In June 2026, Colombia elected the Trump-endorsed outsider Abelardo de la Espriella , and Keiko Fujimori finally won Peru on her fourth attempt. Moreover, Argentina’s right-wing President Javier Milei continues to be an ally.
Tensions between Brazil and the United States have been accumulating in Trump’s second term. In July 2025, the U.S. president imposed tariffs of up to 50 percent on Brazilian goods over the prosecution and later incarceration of Jair Bolsonaro and sanctioned the Supreme Court judge overseeing the case.
On May 26, 2026, Trump received Flavio in the Oval Office, and on June 2, a day after his administration proposed a fresh 25 percent tariff on Brazilian goods, Trump praised him publicly . Flavio asked Washington to postpone the tariffs until after the voting period, but it was too late: a Datafolha poll found that 52 percent of Brazilians saw the tariffs as an effort to help his campaign, but ultimately hurting the Brazilian economy.
Until 2030, Brazil and Mexico, the two largest economies in Latin America, will be governed by center-left leaders, both of whom refuse to pick a clear side between Washington and Beijing. For a doctrine premised on sorting the hemisphere into aligned and unaligned camps, this is a strategic setback for Trump, precisely at a moment where the leader faces low approval rates at home.
Beijing’s Geoeconomic Influence in the Region Is Growing
For China, Brazil is now a strategic partner. In 2025 it was the single largest destination for Chinese outbound investment worldwide, absorbing 10.9 percent of the total, according to the China-Brazil Business Council (CEBC). Chinese investment in China reached $6.1 billion, up 45 percent, far outpacing both Brazil’s overall foreign direct investment (FDI) growth of 4.8 percent and China’s global outbound growth of 1.3 percent .
Overall Brazil accounts for almost two thirds of China’s FDI in South America, with a total stock of $85.5 billion , distributed across 355 projects, between 2007-2025.
China continues to invest heavily in Brazil’s electricity sector, spanning renewable generation and transmission . Automotive investment rose 66 percent to $965 million as BYD began production at the former Ford complex in Camaçari, Bahia (Northeastern Brazil), and Great Wall Motors at the former Mercedes-Benz plant in Iracemápolis, São Paulo. Geely has sealed an alliance with Renault do Brasil and plans local production in Paraná (Southern Brazil) this year.
Beyond investment, bilateral trade hit a record $171 billion in 2025. China bought nearly 80 percent of Brazil’s soybean exports. These ties survived even Jair Bolsonaro’s hostile rhetoric. But a Flavio government that owed its political capital to Washington would have faced intense pressure to slow Chinese investment, and it would have inherited brand-new legal tools to do so (more on this below).
After his loss, Flavio Bolsonaro immediately fled Brazil, heading secretly to the United States via Argentina, amid fears of being convicted of ties to money laundering schemes.
Brazil and the Race for Technology and Critical Minerals
Lula signed Law 15.506/2026 on September 16, creating Brazil’s first National Policy on Critical and Strategic Minerals (PNMCE) and a council, the CIMCE, attached to the presidency. The stakes for investors are considerable: Brazil holds the world’s second-largest rare earth reserves and leads global niobium production, with newly found lithium and nickel reserves.
China still controls roughly 90 percent of rare earth processing and magnet manufacturing and the United States was seeking to secure privileged access to exploration of this sector in the Brazilian market.
The new law has two main aspects: promotion and regulation. The first key is promotion in an industrial policy style. Brazil’s government will provide up to 7 billion Brazilian real in support for firms aiming to raise production and processing of critical minerals, as well as tax credits of up to 1 billion real a year between 2030 and 2034, tied to value-adding and processing on Brazilian soil.
The second aspect is regulation. The newly formed council, led by the president, must approve direct or indirect changes of control in companies holding rights to critical minerals, as well as international supply agreements that could affect Brazil’s economic or geopolitical security.
On paper, this created a screening mechanism that can be used as a hurdle for Chinese state capital, depending on the elected administration. A senior official at the Ministry of Mines and Energy said in October that scrutiny would concentrate on business groups or financing backed by foreign governments, while purely domestic deals may be exempt.
Today, the most visible foreign investors in Brazilian rare earths are American. In April 2026, USA Rare Earth acquired the Serra Verde Mining Complex , Brazil’s only commercial producer of rare earths, for $2.8 billion, in a deal backed by the U.S. government, including $565 million in direct funding from the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation.
Meanwhile, between 2024-2025 three Chinese state-owned enterprises invested more than $1.2 billion in acquisitions of copper, nickel, niobium and lithium mines in Brazil. BYD has held lithium rights in Minas Gerais region since 2023.
Under Lula, the CIMCE is likely to wield screening as an industrial policy filter, asking how much value stays in Brazil. The new law rewards precisely what Chinese firms can offer and Washington struggles to: refining know-how, battery materials capacity, and captive demand from EV plants already operating in Brazil. Under a Flavio government, however, the same powers could easily have been aligned with Washington’s geoeconomic

articles.title_orig: Everything Apple Announced This Week: All About OLED, MacBooks And A Touchscreen
articles.title_zh: Everything Apple Announced This Week: All About OLED, MacBooks And A Touchscreen
articles.content_orig:
In addition to the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display at a "Pro and Tell" event in LA, this week brought us an OLED iPad mini and M6 MBP.
Apple wasn't done with its product reveals for the fall after unveiling the iPhone Duo , iPhone 18 Pro models and an array of smart home devices . Nor could it wait until the third event of the season, dubbed "Pro and Tell," to show off more gear.
The company got a string of announcements underway on Monday with the reveal of the long-awaited OLED iPad mini. Tuesday brought us an M6-powered iMac and 14-inch MacBook Pro. Then, on Wednesday, Apple unveiled its long-anticipated touchscreen MacBook Pro.
Elsewhere, Apple released the latest versions of its operating systems. Among other things, those added more Siri AI features and made the assistant available in more languages. The company updated Apple Creator Studio with more AI features and creative tools as well.
Here's an overview of everything Apple announced this week.
It feels like we've been waiting for forever for Apple to put an OLED display in the iPad mini but that day has finally arrived. The new display has double the peak brightness of the one on the previous model at 1,200 nits, and it has a 2,000,000:1 contrast ratio. The base storage remains the same at 128GB, though if you opt for 256GB or 512GB of storage, you can snag a variant with a nano-texture glass display. That'll cost you extra, naturally.
The company managed to squeeze in a larger screen — an 8.5-inch display rather than the 8.3-inch one in the previous model — without increasing the size of the tablet. In fact, the new iPad mini is slightly narrower than the last one, at 5.22 inches vs. 5.3 inches. It's lighter as well, with the Wi-Fi model coming in at 0.56 pounds (compared with 0.65 pounds last time) and the 5G variant weighing 0.58 pounds (versus 0.66 pounds). The latter, by the way, now boasts Apple's C2 modem, which is said to deliver up to 50 percent faster data speeds than the previous iPad mini. There's also Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread connectivity thanks to the N1 chip.
The OLED iPad mini — the eighth generation of the device — runs on the A20 Pro, the same chipset as the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. Apple says the SoC is capable of running large language models locally, in case you're into that kind of thing. Otherwise, the tablet should be notably faster than earlier models. It supports Apple Intelligence and Siri AI as well, of course. The chipset also boasts a 7-core GPU — two more cores than the A17 Pro, which powered the last-gen iPad mini.
On the camera front, there's a 12MP Center Stage lens on front of the tablet, which Apple has finally shifted to the landscape edge on the iPad mini. However, there's still no Face ID. The 12MP camera on the rear supports 4K 60fps video capture and Smart HDR 4.
The 8th-gen iPad mini has a sealed enclosure to help protect it from the elements. The tablet has an IP67 rating, meaning that it should withstand dust and being immersed in a meter of freshwater for up to 30 minutes, though I would advise against intentionally submerging your iPad mini.
As for battery life, Apple says that should be roughly the same as last time. The company says the new iPad mini should run for up to 10 hours when you're watching video or surfing the web over Wi-Fi. That drops down to nine hours if you're browsing over a cellular connection. If you have at least a 35W power adaptor, you'll be able to recharge the battery to 50 percent of its capacity in 30 minutes, Apple says.
The most interesting thing to me about this iPad mini is that it has Apple's first Acoustic Display, which the company says helps it deliver "an even better audio experience." It claims the tablet offers more volume and "punchier bass" thanks to woofers that "are paired through the display." Apple added that "custom tweeters are now hidden between the glass and aluminum enclosure for clearer highs." I'm definitely curious to find out how all of that sounds in practice.
Inevitably, the latest iPad mini comes with a price hike. It starts at $699, which is $150 more than the previous model after Apple increased the price of that in June . Pre-orders are now open and the tablet will hit shelves on November 6.
On Tuesday, Apple gave the iMac and MacBook Pro spec bumps. The desktop and laptop now each have the M6 chipset , which recently debuted in the Mac mini .
Let's start with the new iMac . Apple says the M6's dual 16-core neural engine enables it to deliver up to five times faster on-device AI performance (for Siri AI, Apple Intelligence and local LLMs) than the previous-gen iMac from 2024 , which had the M4 chipset. The M6 is said to deliver up to 1.5 times faster performance than the M4 for daily tasks, up to two times faster graphics performance (for photo editing etc.) and up to two times higher gaming performance with ray tracing.
The base-level M6 has 10 CPU cores (two super, three performance and two efficiency cores) and a 10-core CPU, compared with eight of each in the M4. There's the option to have a 12-core M6, in which case your desktop will have four Thunderbolt 4 ports instead of the two that the base model has. The four-port model has a nano-texture glass option as well.
Elsewhere, Apple has introduced its N1 networking chip to the iMac. As such, the computer has support for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread connectivity. It also has the option to add a 2.5Gb Ethernet port, an upgrade from gigabit Ethernet on the M4 iMac.
Specs otherwise are the same as last time. You'll still get a 24-inch 4.5K Super Retina display, a 12MP Center Stage camera, a six‑speaker Dolby Atmos system, at least 16GB of RAM and 256GB of base storage. The dimensions are identical too, though the M6 iMac is a touch lighter than the previous gen at 9.7 pounds (versus 9.74 pounds). Don't expect any changes to the color options either — the new iMac is still available in blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange and silver.
One other thing that's staying the same? The starting price, at least after the $200 increase that Apple gave the M4 iMac over the summer. The new model starts at $1,499, and the four-port version will run you at least $1,699. Pre-orders are open and you'll be able to pick one up in store on November 6.
The latest 14-inch MacBook Pro has the 12-core version of the M6 chipset and the N1 networking chip for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support. Those appear to be the only spec changes this time.
Compared with the previous-gen 14-inch MBP, which had an M5 SoC, Apple says the M6 model offers up to 30 percent faster graphics performance and up to 25 percent faster AI workloads. It's said to deliver up to 1.3 faster rendering performance with ray tracing in Blender, up to 1.2 times faster image-processing performance in Affinity and up to 1.3 faster project build performance for compiling code in Xcode.
It doesn't seem like this will be a massive upgrade for folks with an M5 model. However, if you have an older MacBook Pro (or really need those incremental improvements from the previous gen), it might be worth making the switch.
Either way, creatives might want to take note of all the updates that are rolling out for Apple Creative Studio . Apple has given Final Cut Pro a long-awaited quality-of-life upgrade by letting you pull clips from the primary storyline and place them anywhere on the timeline, which seems like very basic functionality to have! MotionVFX is integrated into the app on Mac as well, so you'll have thousands of elements at your fingertips for your video edits.
If you have a Mac that supports Apple Intelligence and is set to US English, Logic Pro has an "intelligent assistant" powered by OpenAI that's available in beta. The app has an an enhanced Stem Splitter that can now separate drums as well. In addition, Keynote, Pages and Numbers now have a chatbot you can use to adjust presentations, documents and spreadsheets.

articles.title_orig: Apple Unveils Touch-Screen MacBook Pro, Reversing Long-Held Jobs Stance
articles.title_zh: Apple Unveils Touch-Screen MacBook Pro, Reversing Long-Held Jobs Stance
articles.content_orig:
Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.
Surpassed only by the iPhone Duo , this year’s most anticipated Apple announcement is its launch of both a 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen display — the company’s last-to-the-party use of both technologies in one of its laptops. And despite the awful name, it’s more than just a fancy new display. It’s really a complete design overhaul that, at least on paper, brings its feature set up to the front of the class for professional content creation, albeit with the same processor options and ports as the other MacBook Pros.
Aside from a screen that brings its capabilities more in line with the Studio Display XDR , the new model adds:
It doesn’t come cheap, though; as predicted, you pay a $400 premium over the standard models. The 14-inch M5 Pro model starts at $2,899 compared to $2,499 for the same non-OLED version, and the M5 Max model begins at $4,499 compared to $4,099. If you want to upgrade to 16TB, you have to bump to the M5 Max — that’s a minimum buy-in of $11,499 with only 36GB of memory. Preorders start today and systems are slated to start shipping Nov. 6.
One of the most popular changes won’t be the whizzy features, but the drop in weight to 3 pounds for the 14-inch model (down from 3.4 pounds) and to 4 pounds (down from 4.7 pounds) for the 16-inch. Also, while Apple updated its sound system to deliver better bass and incorporated Dolby Atmos support to its spatial audio, one of the more notable enhancements is the claimed improvements to the sound when the MacBook is closed.
A lot of the traditional advantages of OLED over alternatives like IPS with array backlights — such as a wider color gamut and true blacks — are less pronounced than they used to be.
That’s even more true for the current MacBook Pro’s mini-LED-backlit Liquid Retina XDR screens: They already deliver excellent deep blacks and 100% P3 gamut coverage, along with great color accuracy sufficient for prosumer creative work.
But the PROLED XDR screen sounds top-notch. While I take Apple’s claim of a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio with 10,000,000 grains of salt — the arithmetic ratio of peak brightness to minimum black isn’t really meaningful, especially beyond about a million — the display has an expanded gamut that covers the Adobe RGB color space and more of Rec. 2020, a space for mastering video.
The latter is still only 80%, but at the moment, that’s the best you can get in a laptop display.
Peak brightness is also similar to the desktop display at 2,000 nits. As with the current screens, though, you can only set the SDR brightness up to 1,000 nits; above that, it’s only automated to compensate for bright sunlight. That can get frustrating for people like me who find auto- brightness distracting.
The display can do 1,000 nits full screen in both SDR and HDR, though. Microsoft’s recently shipped Surface Laptop Ultra also hits 2,000 nits, the first Windows laptop that does, but uses mini-LED.
Oddly, Apple still quotes a 1-nit minimum brightness spec, similar to its mini-LED screens, though OLED’s native minimum is a lot lower: Theoretically, it’s zero, but professional colorimeters have measured it a lot lower. That may be because Apple has adopted it as a standard, and possibly clamped it, to tonally match its mini-LED models.
Apple also refers to its panel technology generically as “tandem OLED,” which is a little annoying, since there is a raft of tandem OLED types. But it is “state of the art!”
There are a couple of potential disappointments, though. For one, the battery life is unchanged. While the MacBook Pro’s battery life has always been good, it’s clear that the OLED display didn’t provide any power savings, or at least savings that weren’t spent elsewhere in the system.
Touch looks like the biggest mixed bag, though. The hardware is only a small aspect of the implementation; operating system interfaces like those of iOS and iPadOS are built around considerations like your finger is bigger and fatter than a cursor. Simply porting the mobile interfaces to a laptop isn’t necessarily a solution, either.
We use laptops in part because a hardware keyboard is sometimes the best input choice, and even navigating the mobile devices via touch can get annoying, so those interfaces don’t necessarily translate optimally.
The point is, a lot is riding on how Apple has adapted MacOS for touch. For instance, the Touch Bar floundered in part because it felt grafted on rather than integral to the OS’ interface, as well as arguably superfluous.
And since Apple didn’t launch the capability with MacOS 27 at its developer conference, WWDC , this year, it sounds like the applications will be behind. That’s not something you beta test on a pro-level production system. Pros rely heavily on muscle memory. It should really have launched with a MacBook Air.
Plus, in order to adapt to touchscreen usage, Apple had to change the hinge to make it stiffer — poking a screen makes that necessary — as well as add image stabilization to the webcam in case you want to poke the screen during video calls.
Apple seemed like it was really stretching to find meaningful uses for touch. Playing piano on a screen that forces your hand to an awkward angle? No thanks. The one application which sounded like it might be okay was for developers to simulate mobile app interfaces.
I was also kind of hoping for increased refresh rates beyond 120Hz or the ability to manually set it above 60Hz. Apple seems to position ProMotion as a power-saving technology rather than for gaming. Apple also seems to think 60fps is a great frame rate, so it’s not surprising.

articles.title_orig: Google announces Gemini 4 Carbon with ‘significant gains across coding and agentic tasks’
articles.title_zh: Google announces Gemini 4 Carbon with ‘significant gains across coding and agentic tasks’
articles.content_orig:
Following the launch of Argon two weeks ago, Google today announced Gemini 4 Carbon as its next frontier model.
There are “significant gains” in coding, agentic tasks, and cybersecurity defense (finding vulnerabilities). Notably, “Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59.”
Google says this fast release is due to its researchers and models “working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster.”
Based on user feedback following the last launch, Google worked to improve Carbon across “coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding.”
On the safety front, Google worked to improve alignment and trained Carbon to “respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way.”
Officially, Gemini 4 Carbon is “coming soon to developers, businesses, and consumers.” The model will first be available to “cyber defenders” this week.
Once available, Google will offer introductory pricing of “$2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price.” Afterward, it will cost $4 per 1M input tokens and $20 per 1M output tokens.

articles.title_orig: China-Vatican deal has imperfections, Vatican’s foreign minister says
articles.title_zh: China-Vatican deal has imperfections, Vatican’s foreign minister says
articles.content_orig:
Archbishop Paul Gallagher acknowledged the agreement’s challenges in a meeting with journalists in Rome.
Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Vatican’s secretary for relations with states and international organizations, acknowledged the challenges of the Vatican-China deal on Tuesday.
Speaking at an event with journalists in Rome, the British diplomat responded to questions regarding the agreement, Pope Leo XIV’s health, and calls for a ceasefire in the ongoing Russo-Ukrainian war.
The full text of the 2018 agreement between China and the Holy See has never been made public. Under the publicly understood terms of the agreement, the pope retains final authority over episcopal appointments in China and may reject candidates proposed by Beijing. The Holy See, for its part, agreed not to appoint bishops without the Chinese government’s prior approval.
As reported by Reuters , Gallagher said that, regarding the agreement, its imperfections were visible.
“Itʼs not easy, the dialogue is not easy,” Gallagher said. “The imperfections of the agreement are ⁠evident, but ​there is a commitment to persevere in dialogue ... and that is what will ​continue to happen.”
He also answered questions regarding a potential visit from Leo to the U.S., saying that it could happen “in the not too distant future.”
Regarding the pope’s Oct. 13 surgery and subsequent recovery, Gallagher described it as a “bit of a game changer” and a revelation of the pope’s mortality, as with every human being.
“[The pope] is a poor mortal like the rest of ​us,” Gallagher said.
In August, Gallagher traveled to Russia to discuss the country’s ongoing war with Ukraine with senior officials. He told journalists that he did not believe the Vatican was involved in discussions of the ceasefire between the two nations.
