articles.title_orig: China's secretive space plane caught on camera in incredible new photo released by US military
articles.title_zh: China's secretive space plane caught on camera in incredible new photo released by US military
articles.content_orig:
A winged Chinese spacecraft bearing a strong resemblance to the US military’s X-37B spaceplane was photographed in orbit by a passing US-owned commercial satellite in 2024, and we finally have the image.
The Chinese spaceplane has delta wings, payload bay doors, a dark heat shield, and a rear-mounted service module with power-generating solar arrays. In other words, the design of the winged ship is, to a great degree, a copy of the X-37B spaceplane flown by the US Space Force.
The photo was taken by a commercial imaging satellite owned by a company called Vantor, known as Maxar in 2024. Vantor is one of several companies that provide reconnaissance imagery of locations around the world to the US military and US intelligence agencies. The same Earth-imaging satellites can point their telescopes at objects in space.
Lower-resolution views of a Chinese spaceplane showing the vehicle’s general shape were publicly available before the DIA assessment. A US Space Force official revealed Maxar’s observation at a 2024 conference in South Korea, but the Pentagon did not release the full-resolution image to the public until Monday, when it appeared in an unclassified Defense Intelligence Agency assessment of threats to the United States in space.
The DIA report doesn’t reveal much new about what the Chinese spaceplane does in orbit. China has launched four spaceplane missions since 2020, with durations of up to nine months. The fourth mission is in orbit today after launching in February. It is not publicly known whether China has one or more such spaceplanes in its inventory.
The Space Force has two X-37Bs flying in rotation, with the longest of their eight missions to date running two-and-a-half years from launch until landing. US officials have released photos of the X-37B vehicles, published information about their design and dimensions, and disclosed a handful of experiments they have carried into orbit. Most of the X-37B’s activities in space are classified.
Like the X-37B, China’s spaceplane lifts off inside the payload shroud of a conventional rocket, then operates as a satellite once in orbit. The spaceplane flies like a miniature unpiloted version of NASA’s Space Shuttle and reenters the atmosphere for an autonomous land runway landing at the end of each mission. Ground teams then refurbish it for another flight.
The “enhanced maneuverability” of spaceplanes makes them “more suitable for certain missions than traditional satellites,” the DIA said in its report. So far, the Chinese spaceplane has only flown in low-Earth orbit (LEO) at an altitude of a few hundred miles. One of the Space Force’s X-37B flights soared to an altitude of more than 24,000 miles before using aerobraking to set up for reentry and landing .
Spaceplanes like China’s and the X-37B can also deploy small satellites from their cargo bay. Most recently, China demonstrated an ability to catch an object in orbit, perhaps using a robotic arm. The vehicle now in space released a sub-satellite in June and recaptured it in July, then did the same thing again in August and September, according to an analysis of open source orbital tracking data by Jonathan McDowell , an astrophysicist who catalogs spaceflight activity.
The official name of the Chinese spaceplane is even a mystery. It is often called Shenlong in Western publications, citing reports from the 2000s about China’s development of a robotic spaceplane. Chinese state media only refer to the vehicle as Chongfu Shiyong Shiyan Hangtian Qi, or CSSHQ, which means reusable experimental spacecraft, according to a fact sheet published by the Secure World Foundation .
The DIA did not disclose the exact circumstances of Maxar’s observation of the Chinese spaceplane, such as its timing, location, or distance, but Earth observations often use cameras to view other objects in space as their orbits intersect, an emerging field known as non-Earth imaging (NEI).
NEI allows commercial operators and government analysts to inspect satellites. This is especially useful for gleaning information about classified or proprietary satellite designs, extending a new avenue for international and corporate espionage to the high frontier.
The capability exhibited by Maxar and other commercial companies in the NEI field is distinct from the recent actions of some military spacecraft, such as Russia’s Kosmos 2612, which deliberately maneuvered to approach a US-registered radar imaging satellite earlier this month. Commercial NEI observations come from chance encounters, often at extremely high speed.
The DIA’s assessment of space threats includes an update on China’s pursuit of anti-satellite technology, or “counterspace” weapons. The intelligence agency reported the Chinese military likely considers directed-energy weapons (DEWs) “ideal counterspace systems” because they can be used to permanently or temporarily disable a satellite. One potential use for lasers in space would be to dazzle a sensor on an adversary’s satellite.
“China has multiple ground-based laser weapons with varying power levels to disrupt, degrade, or damage satellites in LEO,” the DIA said. “By the late 2020s, China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits.”
The DIA noted China’s testing of ground-based anti-satellite missiles and the country’s historic demonstration last year of satellite refueling in geosynchronous orbit, a regime some 22,000 miles (36,000 kilometers) over the equator, something no other country has achieved above LEO. China has also tested a robotic arm that could snag a spacecraft out of orbit, and now operates a growing fleet of satellites called TJS that routinely approach foreign spacecraft.
The US Space Force also has a constellation of inspector satellites in geosynchronous orbit and recently procured more that could be refueled, overcoming maneuverability limitations. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed last month that the Pentagon has fielded weapons in space , making the United States the first nation to acknowledge possession of orbital weapons.
Russia is pursuing its own orbital combat program, which includes an ambition to deploy a nuclear weapon in space, according to US intelligence officials.
A more conventional Russian weapons system, known as Nivelir, is designed to fire projectiles from one satellite to smash into another. The Russian military simulated an attack using the Nivelir system in 2020. In April, Russia launched a fleet of small satellites into an orbit close to a commercial radar remote sensing satellite owned by ICEYE that provides reconnaissance imagery to Ukraine. One of the Russian satellites moved within “tens of meters” of the ICEYE satellite earlier this month before backing away, US officials said.

articles.title_orig: Putin salutes Musk's genius as Russia plays catch-up with Starlink
articles.title_zh: Putin salutes Musk's genius as Russia plays catch-up with Starlink
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk is a "real genius", Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday after revealing the two are in "close" contact about satellite technology.
The remarks came during the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, during which Putin discussed Russia's own satellite internet project Rassvet, which provides internet connections to people from satellites.
"He's a genius, a real genius," Putin said of Musk, according to a translation of his remarks by the BBC. "We are in close contact with our American partners, including Mr. Musk."
Starlink is part of Musk's company SpaceX. The company did not respond to a request for comment.
Putin added that it was important for Russia to be in contact with Musk so Rassvet and Starlink satellites do not "interfere with each other in orbit".
"We and our American partners value this mutually, and despite all the political questions, we are working hard," he said.
Starlink has launched roughly 13,000 of its satellites, according to the company. By contrast there are only a couple of dozen Rassvet satellites currently in orbit, according to online satellite trackers.
The Russian Embassy in South Africa said on Wednesday Rassvet is "Russia's Starlink alternative" and "marks only the country's first steps in this field".
"Russia maintains close contacts with the US on space, including with Elon Musk," the embassy wrote.
Putin's comments about Rassvet and Starlink were made as the US and Russia appear to be growing closer, even as it approaches five years since Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Ukraine relied on Starlink internet in its efforts to keep Russia's forces at bay. But its military last week suddenly suffered Starlink connectivity problems, something Musk has admitted SpaceX did intentionally.
US President Donald Trump earlier this month said he'd struck a deal with Russia to import diesel in an effort to lower gas prices that have skyrocketed due to the US war with Iran.
Then Trump waived certain sanctions against Russia that were set to take effect.
Not long after, a US citizen was released from Russian custody, with US envoy Steve Witkoff referring to Putin as a "humanitarian".
Musk was born in South Africa and then immigrated to Canada before settling in the US. All of his business ventures, including Tesla, SpaceX and Starlink, are based in America, with most operating out of California and Texas.
The billionaire, and off and on again trillionaire, has been one of the biggest political allies and financiers of Trump and other Republican US politicians.

articles.title_orig: Ethiopia says it received Russian Su-35 jets, S-400 air defence systems to follow
articles.title_zh: Ethiopia says it received Russian Su-35 jets, S-400 air defence systems to follow
articles.content_orig:
Ethiopia has received 12 Russian Su-35 fighter jets and will also acquire four S-400 air defence batteries, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has announced.
Abiy made the announcement on X on Wednesday during a visit to Moscow for the two-day Russia-Africa Summit, where Russia is seeking closer security and economic ties with African countries.
The acquisition comes as Ethiopian forces fight renewed battles with rebels in northern Tigray and a separate rebellion in the neighbouring Amhara region.
The prime minister said the warplanes had arrived a year earlier than expected under an existing agreement with Moscow, thanking Russian President Vladimir Putin for helping speed up the delivery.
He gave no date for the arrival of the S-400 batteries, designed to shoot down aircraft and missiles.
Abiy said on Wednesday that the new equipment would strengthen Ethiopia’s ability to “preemptively deter aggression”.
In a second X post later that day, he described the jets as newly deployed and said they would defend Ethiopian airspace.
The announcement is the latest sign of Russia ‘s growing military partnership with Ethiopia, following a series of agreements in recent years.
The two governments signed a military cooperation agreement in Addis Ababa in July 2021 aimed at improving the Ethiopian armed forces’ training and technology.
In January, defence publication Janes reported that Ethiopia had displayed newly acquired Russian Yak-130 advanced jet trainers during celebrations marking its air force’s 90th anniversary.
Russia supplied 15 percent of Africa’s imports of major weapons between 2021 and 2025, making it the continent’s third-largest supplier, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
Moscow has sought closer military and economic ties with African countries while facing Western sanctions over its war in Ukraine.
The Russia-Africa Summit, which began on Wednesday, brings African leaders together for talks on trade, investment and security.
The announcement follows a major shift in the fighting in Tigray, where government troops and allied forces entered the regional capital Mekelle on October 4 after fighters from the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) withdrew.
The TPLF, an armed group that previously governed the region, has suffered further territorial losses as government forces advanced into other towns.
Addis Ababa has since appointed a six-month caretaker administration for Tigray, but the fighting has not stopped.
A TPLF commander called for continued resistance in a television broadcast last week, while the group has also claimed attacks against government-aligned troops in northwestern Tigray on Wednesday.
The renewed war has effectively undone a peace agreement signed in Pretoria, South Africa, in November 2022 that ended two years of fighting, which researchers at Belgium’s Ghent University estimate killed about 500,000 civilians.
Government forces are also battling Fano, an Amhara armed group that has been fighting federal troops since 2023.

articles.title_orig: Nelson Peltz-led group offers to buy Wendy’s for $1.4B
articles.title_zh: Nelson Peltz-led group offers to buy Wendy’s for $1.4B
articles.content_orig:
Bright Lake Wealth Management founder Ted Thatcher analyzes how election anxiety and uncertainty impacts the markets and what it means for investors on 'Varney & Co.'
Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management on Wednesday made an offer to buy Wendy's for roughly $1.4 billion in a move that would make the fast-food chain a privately held company.
Trian has been a long-term shareholder in Wendy's and Peltz's hedge fund is leading a group that offered to buy the struggling fast food giant at a price of $7.35 a share in cash.
The $1.4 billion bid to purchase Wendy's is about a 20% premium over the company's valuation of $1.2 billion at Tuesday's market close.
The offer by the Trian-led group was confirmed by FOX Business and disclosed in a filing on Wednesday. The Wall Street Journal first reported on the offer.
WENDY'S LOSES STATUS AS SECOND-LARGEST BURGER CHAIN AFTER 6-YEAR RUN
Wendy's stock has struggled over the last five years. (Mike Campbell/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Wendy's shares have fallen about 68% over the last five years as of Wednesday's market open, though the stock surged nearly 17% on Wednesday morning following the news.
The Trian-led group bidding to buy Wendy's includes restaurant operator Flynn Group along with investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners.
The group said in a letter that making Wendy's a private company would better allow it to carry out a complicated turnaround process that's expected to take multiple years and entail major capital investment .
MAJOR WENDY'S FRANCHISEE FILES FOR BANKRUPTCY
Nelson Peltz, founder and CEO of Trian Fund Management, said in the letter that Wendy's would be better positioned as a private company. (Marco Bello/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"Wendy's sits at a critical juncture. The external environment has become increasingly challenging given the significant pressures on the U.S. consumer , economic uncertainty, persistent commodity inflation and intensifying competition, particularly with the QSR burger category," the group wrote.
"The business requires significant capital investment to de-lever and execute the strategic initiatives needed to turn system performance around," it added.
WENDY'S TO CLOSE HUNDREDS OF RESTAURANTS AS COMPANY LOOKS TO FOCUS ON VALUE TO BOOST SALES
The letter said that in the group's view, the alternative to accepting the offer to take Wendy's private is "continued exposure to market volatility while the Company works to manage its balance sheet against approaching debt maturities and the significant capital investment needed for the brand, all under the short-term pressure of public markets ."
"We believe private ownership is the better path and provides the patient, long-duration capital needed to restore the business and the franchise system to a position of strength," the group added.

articles.title_orig: Options traders break down a massive Alphabet trade into earnings
articles.title_zh: Options traders break down a massive Alphabet trade into earnings
articles.content_orig:
Options traders took contrasting views on Alphabet as the hyperscaler gets set to report earnings after the close.
Current options prices are implying a nearly 6% move, well about its eight quarter median move of 2.6%. Traders were decidedly bullish heading into the first. Just before noon, a trader bought 2271 contracts of the 350/365 call spread for about $4.4. The trade target a move higher to $365, a 13% jump from its current price. The trade is a bet the in the near term, the worst is behind Alphabet, which has seen its shares fall nearly 20% from its all time highs reached back in May.
Some traders are taking a different tact into the print. Specifically, a separate trader put on a bearish 3x1 put diagonal, collected $1.9M by selling 9,000 of the Nov. 20 expiration 290-strike puts at $4.15 per contract while buying 3,000 of the Jan. 15, 2027 exp. 300-strike puts at $2.15 per contract for a total debit of $2.5M
This is a trade that looks to take advantage of high near-term volatility in Alphabet's shorter dated puts. The goal is for those short-dated puts to expire worthless, with the trader then long the 300-strike puts, looking for a 9% move lower through mid January.
The market's mini rally faces a key test after the bell when tech giants Alphabet and Microsoft report. The technical set-up and options expectations could not be more different.
Microsoft is less than one percent below its closing record reached earlier this month, while Alphabet is flirting with technical bear-market territory, off 20% from its closing high in May. Market-makers are pricing a 5.8% move for Alphabet stock after its report, compared to under a 5% swing for Microsoft, Cboe LiveVol data show. For Microsoft, it's a smaller implied move than its 2-year average swing of 6%. For Alphabet, which has averaged a 2.7% reaction over that time period, it's more than double – which arguably makes sense considering the shares dropped 7% after last quarter's report and rallied 10% the report prior. The ratio of puts to calls on both stocks has been gradually building up on the put side as the Nasdaq 100 Index pulled back, but the metric's baseline for both shows more calls than puts the past year, with a ratio consistently under 1, according to Barchart data. In Microsoft, the ratio is currently 0.59, up from a low of 0.43 in June.
In Alphabet, the ratio is 0.72, the highest since August, but Tuesday's options flows cast a more positive light. Of the 435,000 options traded, 312,00 were calls, with almost 102,000 call trades likely initiated by buyers, versus just 54,000 by sellers and the remaining near the mid-price, Cboe data show. Some of the heaviest call-buying in Alphabet was at the 360-strike for January expiry, where it looked like a single trader bought around $18.5 million of calls across eight transactions of 2,850 contracts each, SpotGamma data show.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu defies exit polls to take lead in Israeli election — what it means for Iran war
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu defies exit polls to take lead in Israeli election — what it means for Iran war
articles.content_orig:
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu casts his ballot, alongside his wife Sara, at a polling station in Jerusalem on Oct. 27, 2026.
Israel appears to be on the brink of a political deadlock, with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main rival, former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot , projected to gain a parliamentary majority. While partial results show that Netanyahu's Likud party has edged ahead slightly, if the embattled leader is to forge a path for another term, he will likely need to secure a coalition. Such alliances can take weeks or months to form, meaning the future leadership of Israel’s parliament, the Knesset, remains unclear.
As of Wednesday evening in Israel, authorities had counted more than 88% of ballots cast at polling stations across the country. Another set of ballots logged at special polling sites, including military bases, have yet to be counted. Authorities estimate that somewhere between 430,000 and 480,000 votes were cast in this way. As such, it could still take another day or two for the final election results to be released.
Israel's three leading broadcasters have projected that Netanyahu's bloc of right-wing parties is on course to win 53 seats in parliament, with the opposition ‌bloc of Eisenkot looking at 48. Both are short of the 61 seats required for a majority. Parties representing Arab Israelis are projected to secure 19 seats.
Once all the votes have been tallied, Netanyahu looks set to remain as caretaker while President Isaac Herzog holds consultations with all the political factions to determine the formation of the next government—a process that could take weeks.
"Next week, I will invite the representatives of the factions to consultations ahead of assigning the mandate to form the next government," Herzog said on Wednesday. "With the publication of the results, I ask one important thing from everyone who arrives—arrive with an open mind."
Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have stated their own intentions to form the next coalition. In a defiant speech made after the polls closed, Netanyahu called for a "strong, right-wing" government."
Eisenkot, in a social media update late Wednesday, said: "Long workdays still await us, but we are focused on the heavy task entrusted to us—bringing change to Israel and establishing a Zionist mobilization government."
While results remain inconclusive, Netanyahu’s longstanding ally, U.S. President Donald Trump , who gave a last-minute endorsement to the longest-serving Israeli premier, already appeared to take credit for Netanyahu’s election performance.
“You know, it's pretty close, which was very well,” Trump said when asked about it by reporters early Wednesday. “Because I think when the endorsement went out, it helped him a lot, but I actually heard he did pretty well. It might be winning or tie. The tie is sort of considered a win in that case because it’s a big chess match.”
Israelis flocked to polling stations on Tuesday to decide Netanyahu’s political fate . The election was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership and Israelis’ willingness to change course amid uncertainty.
It was the first election in the country since the Oct. 7, 2023 terrorist attacks by Palestinian militant group Hamas and the subsequent Israeli war in the Gaza Strip . Since then, Israel under Netanyahu has pursued an aggressive military campaign across the Middle East—going to war with Iran , backing settler attacks and displacement in the West Bank, and carrying out strikes against militant groups in Lebanon and Yemen
From 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. local time on Tuesday (1 a.m. to 4 p.m. EDT), Israelis were able to cast votes for representatives in the Knesset. Numbers from Israel's Central Elections ​Committee reflected a strong turnout, with 77.7% of eligible voters reported to have cast their ballots by 10 p.m., local time—the highest turnout logged since 1999.
Netanyahu was joined by his wife Sara as he cast his own ballot at a polling station in a Jerusalem school. “This is a very moving and fateful moment. My wife and I are truly overwhelmed,” Netanyahu told reporters after voting. “We know what is at stake, and since I am not allowed to say things explicitly, I will say: Vote correctly.”
Not long after, Netanyahu told his supporters that "buses are heading to the polling stations and huge lines are being reported in the Arab settlements." Complaining that "the right-wing strongholds are not waking up," he again urged people to go out and vote. Netanyahu’s Likud party said in a statement that it had submitted a request to the Central Elections Committee to extend voting hours past 10 p.m. The committee later announced it would not be extending voting hours past the scheduled closing time.
Read More: Israel's Choice
As the vote count continues, here’s what to know about the pivotal election—and what comes next.
Two main political blocs are contending to form Israel’s next government. The first is the pro-Netanyahu coalition led by Netanyahu’s Likud party. The coalition includes far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties, such as Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) led by national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Religious Zionism-Zehut led by finance minister Bezalel Smotrich. Their ultranationalist policies have found an audience in younger right-wing Israelis.
On the other side are the Jewish-led opposition movements—with Eisenkot and the centrist Yashar (Straight) party at the forefront. Eisenkot, who entered politics in 2022, joined Netanyahu’s emergency war cabinet after the Oct. 7 attack on Israel. But after having lost a son in combat in Israel’s wars, Eisenkot left his post in 2024. Two of his nephews also died fighting in Gaza, a prominent campaign talking point.
The opposition also includes a joint ticket led by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and Knesset opposition leader Yair Lapid, the secular nationalist party Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Our Home) led by former finance minister Avigdor Lieberman, and the Democrats led by former IDF deputy chief of staff Yair Golan.
The Democrats party on Tuesday said Golan had been “approached in a threatening manner” by a man who was found to be carrying a knife. The lawmaker was attending a voting-day mobilization tour in Tel Aviv's HaMesila Park at the time of the incident.
"Golan’s security guards blocked the man, and as they moved toward him, a large knife slipped from beneath his clothing and fell to the ground," the party said in a statement shared with the Guardian . "Police were called to the scene and arrested the suspect." Golan, in his own statement, vowed that "incitement and violence will not deter us" and encouraged people to go out and vote.
Meanwhile, some polls had suggested that Eisenkot’s Yashar party may garner slightly more support than Netanyahu’s Likud, but they also projected that neither the Prime Minister’s right-wing bloc nor the opposition were likely to win the 61 Knesset seats needed to form a government.
Including Arab parties such as United Arab List (Ra’am) and the Joint List, or fringe parties, could be necessary to form a government. Both pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu coalitions have so far ruled out teaming up with the Arab-led parties. Arab citizens of Israel make up about 20% of the population, though they receive fewer government services and endure higher poverty and unemployment rates . Discrimination and disappointment have historically depressed Arab-Israeli voter turnout. However, on Tuesday, there appeared to be strong turnout in some of Israel’s largest Arab-majority towns.

articles.title_orig: EU removes mention of ‘associate membership’ from Canada declaration
articles.title_zh: EU removes mention of ‘associate membership’ from Canada declaration
articles.content_orig:
BRUSSELS — EU countries have dropped the idea of offering Canada "associate member" status in the 27-member bloc, opting instead for softer language promising "ever closer association" ahead of a landmark EU-Canada summit, according to the latest version of the draft statement, seen by POLITICO.
A group of countries including Germany, Greece and France all objected to mentioning associate membership in a joint EU-Canada statement to be issued in Montreal, the diplomats said.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen had originally proposed "associate membership" for Canada in her State of the European Union speech in September, catching some EU countries off-guard.
A previous draft of the joint statement had read that the EU and Canada would "work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada Summit the concept of Associate Member that will reflect, through this even closer association, our common endeavour and cooperation towards our shared goals of prosperity, economic security and strategic autonomy."
In the final version, the text reads: "We will create an even closer association between Canada and the EU... and work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada Summit the concept of an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself."
Later in the statement, the language changes from "even closer" to "ever closer." The text still needs final approval. EU countries have a deadline of 6 p.m. to raise objections.
While countries disagree over the wording to describe the relationship, Brussels is not softening its offering to Canada of a vastly expanded partnership.
“The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday. "What matters is the difference that it will make to lives of Canadians."
This story has been updated.

articles.title_orig: iOS 27.2 just upgraded Apple Photos in two ways, here’s what’s new
articles.title_zh: iOS 27.2 just upgraded Apple Photos in two ways, here’s what’s new
articles.content_orig:
Apple Photos got a lot of new features in iOS 27 last month, but this week’s release of iOS 27.2 brought even more improvements. Here’s what’s new.
Shared Albums are among my favorite features in the Photos app. I don’t post on social media often, but I love using Shared Albums because they provide a social media-style experience in a private way that lives right inside Photos.
iOS 27 brought a variety of big improvements to Shared Albums. And now iOS 27.2 has introduced four more.
Per Apple’s release notes , here’s what’s new:
To get these new features, you’ll need to make sure your Shared Albums have been upgraded for iOS 27.
One complication introduced by AI is that it can be hard to know if an image is real or AI-generated.
This challenge extends to AI-edited photos too, which might have key details changed by tools like iOS 27’s Extend, Reframe, and Clean Up features in Photos.
Apple is tackling the issue with its new Reference Image feature in iPhone 18 Pro, and also through a software enhancement that rolled out in iOS 27.2.
Per Apple , its latest software update adds the following:
Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground
SynthID is a cross-platform standard developed by Google that embeds unnoticeable digital watermarks into AI-modified photos. Users won’t see a visible watermark, but anyone who checks for a SynthID marker will find it.
What do you think of the latest Apple Photos changes in iOS 27.2? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_zh: This is how badly X wants you to pay to promote your posts
articles.content_orig:
You have to hand it to X’s latest promotional gimmick.﻿
You have to hand it to X’s latest promotional gimmick.﻿
After Elon Musk warned that “advertisers who post ads that are ugly, shrill, strident or overstate claims about their product will be barred from advertising” on X earlier this month, the platform now appears to be using a jarring animated arm that reaches across the screen to draw attention to the “promote” button while users are composing a post.
Many X users have seen and shared images of the unsettling promotional tool, including The Verge’s Tom Warren , but it doesn’t appear for everyone on the platform. The arm seems limited to verified users, or those with a paid subscription to X Premium. Reactions, unsurprisingly, have been less than positive. “I’ve never promoted a post and HATE this screen takeover,” said Sheel Mohnot , while Jesse Middleton likened it to a Halloween prank. “I wish I could explain how jarring this hand and animation was in the @X app. It was truly shocking, almost like a Halloween gag, but I’m pretty sure it was real.”
Using the paid promote feature extends the reach of an X post to a larger audience based on their location, interests, or demographics, including those not currently following a user’s account. Posts that have been promoted look like other posts on X but are branded with a “promoted” or “ad” label.

articles.content_orig:
Liu was among China’s most prominent female officials in recent decades
Former Chinese vice-premier Liu Yandong died of illness on Wednesday at the age of 80. She was one of China’s most prominent female leaders, playing a pivotal role in the country’s united front work and education sector.
The official obituary released by Xinhua described Liu as an “outstanding leader in the [Communist] Party’s united front work, in China’s education, science and technology, healthcare, and women and children’s affairs.”
Liu was vice-premier from 2013 to 2018. She was the fourth woman to serve in that role.

articles.title_orig: Chinese drug sector’s stature grows at major cancer conference
articles.title_zh: Chinese drug sector’s stature grows at major cancer conference
articles.content_orig:
Hansoh Pharmaceutical, Akeso and others tout positive results as Chinese research accounts for larger percentage of presentations
An array of Chinese drug makers showcased positive trial results for new cancer treatments at a major European medical conference, underscoring the expanding international influence of China’s biotech sector.
Domestic innovative drugs, particularly antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), delivered impressive data across multiple tumour types at the European Society for Medical Oncology (Esmo) Congress, with some early-stage data further showing the country’s “innovation capabilities”, said analysts from China Post Securities in a note on Monday.
Chinese research accounted for 29 of 96 late-breaking abstracts (LBAs) – summaries of newly available clinical research data – presented at the prominent industry conference, held in Madrid from October 23 to 27. Five of the 12 studies selected for the prestigious presidential symposium were also from Chinese firms.

articles.title_orig: Researchers Propose New Irrigation to Balance Water Conservation, Food security in China
articles.title_zh: Researchers Propose New Irrigation to Balance Water Conservation, Food security in China
articles.content_orig:
A new study shows that China may better balance water conservation, food security and investment returns by adopting more efficient irrigation strategies, and expanding irrigated farmland only where conditions are optimal.
The study, published in the journal Nature Food, was led by researchers at the Institute of Atmospheric Physics (IAP) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Hohai University and Xiamen University, in collaboration with several other Chinese and international institutions.
As rising temperatures and droughts put more pressure on food production systems, irrigation is becoming more important for farmers adapting to climate change. But expanding irrigated farmland further burdens already limited water supplies. The researchers therefore look for ways to save water, protect cereal production and improve investment returns all at once.
The team examined 42,190 county-level agricultural statistical records, 3,576 household socioeconomic survey responses and 2,230 irrigation technology comparison trials. It also focused on China's three staple crops: maize, wheat and rice.
The study found that China's agricultural irrigation underwent a significant technological transition between 2010 and 2022. In 2010, earthen-channel water delivery and flood irrigation were still widespread. By 2022, these inefficient practices had declined substantially, while water-saving technologies had become more common. However, the pace of change varied widely across crops and regions.
Wang Jinxia, a professor at Hohai University in east China's Jiangsu Province, said upgrading irrigation and water-saving technologies has long been a key part of China's farmland water conservancy investment.
Wang explained that at the current rate of technology adoption, irrigation water use per area for the three staple crops is projected to fall by only 9.4 percent to 16 percent by 2030. This projected reduction would fall short of the 25.5 percent water-saving target set by the national agricultural sustainable development plan for 2015 to 2030. The plan sets a cap of 373 cubic kilometers on national agricultural irrigation water use by 2030.
The study showed that deploying the most efficient irrigation technologies across all existing irrigated areas could more than meet the water-saving target. However, even such widespread upgrades would not be enough to offset possible crop yield losses caused by future climate change, posing risks to food security.
The researchers therefore proposed a new approach: first improve water-use efficiency in existing irrigated areas, and then, within water resource constraints, use the water saved to convert some rainfed farmland into irrigated farmland. The strategy aims to reduce the adverse effects of future climate change.
The study also found different optimal strategies for the three crops. For maize, the preferred approach is to adopt more advanced irrigation technologies while moderately expanding irrigated areas. For wheat and rice, less expansion is needed, and medium-efficiency water-saving technologies in newly developed irrigated areas could be enough to ensure food security under future climate conditions, meet water-saving policy targets and maximize investment returns.
Zhang Tianyi, a senior scientist at IAP, said the real question policymakers need to answer is which crops need irrigation, where irrigated area should be expanded, by how much, what technologies should be adopted and whether the investments are economically viable.
He noted that previous studies had largely focused on projecting changes in irrigated areas without fully accounting for interactions among irrigation technologies or between existing and newly developed irrigated areas.
"By integrating multi-source data and developing a new analytical framework, the study aims to provide more actionable scientific evidence for these specific investment decisions," he said.
The researchers emphasized that irrigation is not the only solution. Agricultural production is also influenced by crop variety breeding, cultivation management, land management scale and other factors. Irrigation investment should therefore be coordinated with the development of stress-tolerant crop varieties, climate-resilient cultivation practices and the construction of high-standard farmland.
Chen Huang, a researcher from Xiamen University in east China's Fujian Province, said the study drew on three independent datasets collected through different survey and research approaches. Despite their different sources, the model was able to capture the decline in agricultural irrigation water use and the improvement in irrigation productivity in China over the past decade.
"Future research will further incorporate agricultural policy and economic factors such as farmland consolidation and changes in agricultural commodity prices to refine the assessment of irrigation investment," he said. (Xinhua)
Coupling irrigation technology upgrades with targeted expansion enables water-efficient and climate-resilient cereal production in China

articles.title_orig: China Spaceplane CSSHQ: 3 Missions, 8,500 kg [2026]
articles.title_zh: China Spaceplane CSSHQ: 3 Missions, 8,500 kg [2026]
articles.content_orig:
A new Ars Technica report argues that China’s spaceplane cannot hide in low-Earth orbit , and the claim lands at a moment when the program is drawing more public attention than at any point since its first flight in September 2020. The vehicle at the center of the story carries the official name “reusable experimental spacecraft.” Its Chinese name is Chongfu Shiyong Shiyan Hangtian Qi, shortened to CSSHQ.
The headline framing is punchy, but the public record is more modest. The Secure World Foundation describes the CSSHQ as a technology demonstrator and experimental vehicle. Public listings show launches in September 2020, August 2022 and December 2023, with a fourth mission recorded for February 2026. The secrecy implied by the word “top-secret” is something we cannot confirm from the sources we retrieved. That gap between headline and evidence is the real story, and this analysis walks through both sides.
Why does it matter for a hardware audience? Because a reusable vehicle that releases small satellites, flies close to them and comes home is a test bed for sensors, guidance computers, thermal protection and launch integration. It also arrives while commercial launch cadence is climbing fast, as our report on SpaceX tying the California launch record with its 71st Vandenberg flight shows. More traffic in low orbit means more eyes on every object up there, including this one.
Don't miss new tech stories on Google
Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.
Start with the cleanest layer of facts. The Secure World Foundation, a space policy nonprofit, calls the CSSHQ a technology demonstrator. Its assessment says the craft deployed a small satellite during each of its first three missions, and that it performed limited rendezvous and proximity operations with the satellites it released. Those statements form the backbone of everything public about the program.
The mission list is just as plain. Public records place the first three launches in September 2020, August 2022 and December 2023, all on the CZ-2F/T launch vehicle. A search record adds a fourth mission in February 2026. A catalog entry lists an orbit of 332 km by 348 km, inclined 50.20 degrees, for a spacecraft of 8,500 kg.
Now the other layer. Several details that circulate around this story are unconfirmed in the retrieved sources. They include the “top-secret” label, the claim that the vehicle “can’t hide,” and any specific photograph, photographer or commercial satellite imaging event from 2024. Outlets including Ars Technica, TWZ, The Aviationist, Popular Science and Starlust.org have covered the story. The imaging details surfaced in one outlet’s search result, and none of the other retrieved sources confirms them. We treat them as reported claims, not settled fact.
This distinction shapes how a careful reader should handle the China spaceplane story. A craft can be tightly controlled by its operator and still be openly cataloged, because tracking networks log anything that reaches orbit. “Secret” often describes the mission goals, not the existence of the object. That reading fits the evidence far better than the dramatic version.
The acronym CSSHQ comes straight from the Chinese name, Chongfu Shiyong Shiyan Hangtian Qi, which translates as reusable experimental spacecraft. The English phrase matters. It tells you that the program office, at least in public, frames the vehicle as an experiment first. Wikipedia’s entry on the Chinese reusable experimental spacecraft collects the public mission history, and the Secure World Foundation uses the same experimental label.
Press and social media often call it a spaceplane. That shorthand is understandable, since the concept resembles a small winged orbiter that launches on a rocket, spends time in orbit and returns to land. But the fact sheet we rely on does not confirm the vehicle’s dimensions, wing geometry or landing method. We can say that the program describes a reusable spacecraft. We cannot responsibly describe its shape.
What about the owner? The retrieved sources do not name a manufacturer or a formal operator. They also do not state a price, a payload capacity or detailed mission objectives beyond the experimental role. Analysts who fill those blanks are drawing inferences. Some inferences are reasonable, yet none is a documented fact.
For readers who track the broader hardware industry, the naming is a useful clue about intent. A program that stresses reuse is chasing lower cost per flight and faster turnaround, the same pressures driving commercial rockets. A program that stresses experimentation is gathering data, not fielding a service. The CSSHQ sits firmly in the second camp for now.
Four launches over roughly five and a half years is a slow cadence by any standard. The gaps between the first three missions run close to two years, then about sixteen months. The fourth entry, dated February 2026, follows the December 2023 flight by a little over two years. That is arithmetic on public listing dates, not a claim about internal schedules.
Look closely at the fourth row. The verified material confirms the launch vehicle only for the first three missions. It does not confirm whether the February 2026 flight used the same rocket, whether it released a satellite, or whether the vehicle has landed. Any article that states those points as fact goes beyond the evidence we can verify.
That limit matters because the most dramatic claims in circulation attach to the newest flight. Reports of maneuvers and repeated releases deserve attention, and readers should check the outlets directly. Still, a responsible summary separates the three well-documented missions from the one whose details remain thin.
One entry in the Skyrocket space catalog record for the CSSHQ lists an orbit of 332 km by 348 km, with an inclination of 50.20 degrees, for an 8,500 kg spacecraft. Treat it as one catalog entry, not a universal description of every mission. The retrieved material does not say which flight the figures belong to, and orbits change over a mission.
Even so, the numbers carry useful information. A perigee of 332 km and an apogee of 348 km put the craft in a nearly circular orbit, with just 16 km separating the low and high points. The mean altitude works out to 340 km. That is deep in low-Earth orbit, where residual atmosphere drags on any object and where operators need propulsion to hold altitude over long stays.
The last three rows are our own calculations, labeled as such. At a mean radius of about 6,711 km from Earth’s center, standard Kepler math gives a period near 91 minutes. That means roughly 15 to 16 laps around the planet each day. The 50.20 degree inclination means the ground track sweeps latitudes up to about 50 degrees north and south, which covers most of the populated world.
The Ars Technica headline rests on a physical truth that has nothing to do with this one program. Objects in low orbit move fast, cross the sky in minutes and repeat their passes on a predictable schedule. Anyone with the right sensors can log them. Radar networks, telescopes and radio receivers all work on this problem, and low orbits are the easiest to observe because the targets are closest.
An 8,500 kg craft is big. If the catalog mass is right, it outweighs many commercial satellites several times over, and size helps ground trackers. Large objects reflect more sunlight and return stronger radar echoes. Sensor technology on the ground keeps improving too, which we saw in our look at counter-drone tests covering four sensor types , where radar, radio-frequency, optical and acoustic detection each filled different gaps.
The word “hide” still deserves care. A tracker can see that an object exists and where it flies without learning what it does. Orbit data reveals position and maneuvers. It does not reveal payload contents, onboard software or intent. So the headline’s claim and the program’s secrecy can both be par
